newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan markets plunge on China, pork ban.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan markets plunge on China, pork ban.

text.p: Taiwan's share prices and local dollar plunged on Monday over jitters raised by a newspaper report that China would stage war games aimed at protesting the Taiwan visit by exiled Tibetan spiritual leader the Dalai Lama.

Although mainland officials subsequently cast doubt on the report, securities analysts said Taiwan's bourse, plagued by a number of bearish factors, would continue a long profit-taking descent that could erase dramatic gains achieved over 1997.

Even if tensions with China did not materialise, they said, economic concerns over an all-out ban on pork exports following an outbreak of hog foot-and-mouth disease would continue to dampen trading in the local bourse.
"Many investors worry that the disease will have a sharp impact on the overall economy," said Lin Long-hsien, a market analyst for United Securities.
"They will be watching closely to see what kind of stabilising measures the government launches."

Analysts said the benchmark index, which soared 23 percent in a 1997 bull run that peaked with a six-year high of 8,526.20 on March 18, could ease to the 7,500 level before seeing a significant rebound.
"Although share prices are not likely to see another sudden fall, they are still facing strong profit-taking pressure," said Eric Liu, senior analyst for National Securities.
"The index may fall as low as 7,500 in the next two weeks," Liu said.

The stock market plummeted 3.49 percent or 287.19 points to close at 7,946.88 in its biggest single-day drop since the last round of military tensions with arch rival China in early 1996, when it fell 346.74 points on January 5, 1996.
The Taiwan dollar also saw a sharp decline, closing at T$27.625 against its U.S. counterpart against Saturday's T$27.545 finish.

The United Daily News quoted military intelligence as saying China planned April joint-forces war games in coastal Fujian, Guangdong and Zhejiang provinces -- those nearest to Taiwan -- and that the exercises could amount to a protest over a visit to Taiwan by Tibet's exiled spiritual leader, the Dalai Lama.
A Fujian province official told Reuters after the Taiwan stock market closed that he had not heard of any such plans.
Chinese central government comment was not available.
By most accounts, the pork crisis is the paramount concern.
Central bank governor Sheu Yuan-dong told parliament on Monday the pork export ban could slash up to 0.5 percentage points from Taiwan's 1997 gross domestic product growth.
Foreign exchange dealers said the export ban would trap the Taiwan dollar in a downtrend.
"If exports get hurt, the local currency also would take a hit," said one dealer at a foreign bank. She said she expected the rate to sink as low as T$27.8 in one week.
Taiwan has said it must import US$200 million worth of foot and mouth vaccines to ease gaping local shortages.
President Lee Teng-hui announced on Saturday the government would offer up to T$10 billion (US$360 million) in low-interest loans to pork processing companies to help defray losses.

Both the stock market and the Taiwan dollar were dealt an extra blow on Monday by reports that Morgan Stanley has advised its Taiwan investors to reduce portfolio weighting for Taiwan shares to four percent from the current six percent.
